question: State the formula for calculating gross profit.

points: Gross profit = Revenue − Cost of goods sold / Cost of sales (1)

question: State the formula for calculating net profit.

mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept: Revenue − Cost of sales − Expenses.

question: Give two examples of non-current assets that would appear on a Statement of Financial Position (SFP).
Identify two current liabilities that would appear on a Statement of Financial Position.

points: Short-term loans due within one year (1)

question: State the formula for straight-line depreciation.

points: Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life in years (1)
The asset's net book value decreases by the same amount each year (1)

question: State how the reducing balance method of depreciation works.

points: A fixed percentage is applied to the net book value (NBV) of the asset each year (1)
The depreciation charge falls each year as the NBV decreases (1)

question: State the formula for gross profit margin.
Give the formula for net profit margin and state what it measures.

points: Measures the percentage of revenue that remains as net profit after all expenses have been deducted (1)

question: State the formula for the current ratio and explain what a ratio of less than 1 indicates.

points: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities (1)
A ratio below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets — the business may struggle to meet its short-term debts (1)

question: State the formula for the acid test ratio and explain why it excludes inventory.

points: Acid test ratio = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities (1)
Inventory is excluded because it may not be easily or quickly converted into cash (1)

question: State the formula for Return on Capital Employed (ROCE).

points: Capital employed = Total assets − Current liabilities / Non-current liabilities + Equity (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any equivalent correct formula for capital employed.

question: State the formula for mark-up and explain how it differs from gross profit margin.

points: Mark-up = (Gross profit ÷ Cost of goods sold) × 100 (1)
Mark-up is calculated on cost; gross profit margin is calculated on selling price / revenue (1)

question: Identify two components of equity that might appear in the equity section of a Statement of Financial Position.
Give two examples of expenses that would appear in the expenses section of an income statement (below gross profit).
State one advantage of straight-line depreciation over reducing balance depreciation.

points: Straight-line is simpler to calculate (1) as the same amount is charged every year rather than recalculating on a changing NBV (1)
Straight-line gives consistent depreciation charges (1) making financial planning and budgeting more predictable (1)

scenario: TileWorld Ltd has a gross profit margin of 42% this year compared to 51% last year.
question: Explain two possible reasons for the fall in TileWorld Ltd's gross profit margin.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The cost of goods sold may have risen (e.g. higher material or supplier costs) (1) while TileWorld was unable to pass the full cost increase onto customers through higher prices (1)
TileWorld may have reduced its selling prices to attract more customers (1) which would reduce the margin made on each unit sold (1)
A change in product mix — selling a higher proportion of lower-margin products (1) would drag down the overall gross profit margin (1)

scenario: ClearGlass Ltd's current ratio is 0.7:1. Its acid test ratio is 0.3:1.
question: Explain what these ratios indicate about ClearGlass Ltd's financial health.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each ratio. Maximum 4 marks.
points: A current ratio of 0.7:1 means current liabilities exceed current assets (1); ClearGlass may struggle to pay its short-term debts when they fall due (1)

An acid test of 0.3:1 is very low, indicating ClearGlass is heavily reliant on inventory to meet its current liabilities (1); most of its current assets are tied up in stock that may not be quickly sold for cash (1)

scenario: HeavyHaul Ltd bought a truck for £60,000. It will last 6 years and have a residual value of £6,000.
question: Explain why depreciation is charged on the truck and calculate the annual straight-line depreciation charge.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for the explanation and 1+1 for the calculation.
points: Depreciation is charged to spread the cost of the truck over its useful life (1) matching the cost to the periods in which the truck generates revenue, following the accruals accounting principle (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award both calculation marks for correct method and answer.

scenario: LastMile Ltd's ROCE fell from 18% to 11% over two years. Capital employed remained unchanged at £400,000.
question: Explain two possible causes of the fall in ROCE.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each cause. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Net profit may have fallen (1) perhaps due to rising costs or lower revenue, as ROCE = net profit / capital employed × 100 — if profit falls while capital employed stays the same, ROCE falls (1)
Higher expenses such as depreciation, increased wages or rising loan interest (1) would reduce net profit and therefore reduce the ROCE ratio (1)

scenario: PrimeTech Ltd's SFP shows: non-current assets £320,000; current assets £85,000; current liabilities £40,000; non-current liabilities £120,000.
question: Explain what PrimeTech Ltd's net assets are and what this tells us about the business.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for calculation and 1+1 for interpretation.
points: Net assets of £245,000 represents the equity / net worth of the business (1); it shows what shareholders' funds amount to and is an indicator of financial strength (1)

topic: F4 Ratio analysis — mark-up vs margin
scenario: A retailer buys a product for £40 and sells it for £56.
question: Explain the difference between the mark-up and gross profit margin for this product.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for mark-up and 1+1 for GPM.
points: Mark-up = (£16 ÷ £40) × 100 = 40% (1); this measures profit as a percentage of the cost price (1)
Gross profit margin = (£16 ÷ £56) × 100 = 28.6% (1); this measures gross profit as a percentage of the selling price / revenue (1)

scenario: MegaCut Ltd purchased a machine for £50,000. It depreciates using the reducing balance method at 20% per year.
question: Explain the reducing balance depreciation for the first two years and calculate the net book value at the end of Year 2.

points: The charge falls each year because the percentage is applied to a decreasing NBV (1)
Reducing balance method results in higher depreciation charges early in the asset's life — appropriate for assets that lose value quickly (1)

scenario: CozyHome Ltd's income statement shows: Revenue £480,000; Cost of sales £288,000; Gross profit £192,000; Expenses £145,000; Net profit £47,000.
question: Explain what the gross profit margin and net profit margin tell us about CozyHome Ltd's performance.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each ratio. Maximum 4 marks.
points: GPM = (£192,000 ÷ £480,000) × 100 = 40% (1); CozyHome keeps 40p of every £1 of revenue after cost of sales — this is the margin available to cover expenses (1)
NPM = (£47,000 ÷ £480,000) × 100 = 9.8% (1); only 9.8p of every £1 of revenue becomes net profit after all expenses — this seems relatively low, suggesting high expenses relative to revenue (1)

scenario: BuildSafe Ltd has a current ratio of 0.85:1.
question: Explain two actions BuildSafe Ltd could take to improve its current ratio.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each action. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Chase debtors / trade receivables for payment sooner (1) which increases current assets without increasing liabilities, improving the ratio (1)
Convert short-term borrowing (overdraft) to a long-term loan (1) which reduces current liabilities and increases the current ratio (1)
Arrange a sale-and-leaseback of a non-current asset (1) to generate cash (a current asset), improving the current ratio (1)

scenario: Two competing firms: AlphaRetail — GPM 55%, NPM 4%; BetaRetail — GPM 35%, NPM 18%.
question: Explain what these ratios suggest about the cost structures of AlphaRetail and BetaRetail.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each firm. Maximum 4 marks.
points: AlphaRetail has a high GPM (55%) but a very low NPM (4%) (1) suggesting its cost of sales is low but it has very high operating expenses (wages, rent, marketing etc.) that consume most of the gross profit (1)
BetaRetail has a lower GPM (35%) but a high NPM (18%) (1) suggesting higher production/cost of sales but very well-controlled operating expenses (1)

scenario: SolarTech Ltd bought a machine on 1 January Year 1 for £84,000. Estimated useful life: 7 years. Residual value: £7,000.
question: Calculate the annual straight-line depreciation charge and the net book value at the end of Year 3. Show your working. (4)

points: Accumulated depreciation by end of Year 3 = 3 × £11,000 = £33,000 (1)

question: Calculate the following ratios for BluePeak Ltd. Show your working: (i) Gross profit margin; (ii) Net profit margin; (iii) ROCE; (iv) Current ratio; (v) Acid test ratio. (5)

question: Calculate the gross profit margin and the mark-up for StreetEats Ltd. Show your working. (4)

points: Mark-up is higher than GPM because it is calculated on the lower cost figure rather than the higher revenue figure (1)

scenario:
SkyTiles Ltd — two-year comparison:
Year 1: Revenue £500k, GPM 48%, NPM 12%, Current ratio 2.1:1, ROCE 16%.
Year 2: Revenue £620k, GPM 41%, NPM 6%, Current ratio 1.3:1, ROCE 9%.
question: Discuss the financial performance and position of SkyTiles Ltd over the two years. (6)

indicative_content: Revenue grew 24% — positive; but profitability ratios have deteriorated significantly
GPM fell from 48% to 41% — cost of sales has risen as a proportion of revenue
NPM fell from 12% to 6% — expenses have also grown faster than revenue; double squeeze on profitability
ROCE fell from 16% to 9% — capital is generating less return
Current ratio fell from 2.1 to 1.3 — still above 1 so liquidity is adequate but tightened
Revenue growth is not converting to profit — suggests cost control issues
Conclusion: revenue growth is encouraging but profitability and ROCE deterioration is a concern; needs investigation of rising costs

level_descriptors.descriptor: Identifies some changes; little analysis of implications.
Analyses two or more ratios with development; partial conclusion.
Thorough, balanced analysis across all ratios; explains underlying reasons; justified conclusion.

scenario: FastTrack Logistics has just purchased 10 delivery vans at £28,000 each. Finance director Amir is deciding between straight-line depreciation (over 5 years, residual value £3,000 each) and reducing balance at 30% per year.
question: Discuss which depreciation method Amir should choose for the delivery vans. (6)

indicative_content: Straight-line: annual charge = (£28,000 − £3,000) ÷ 5 = £5,000/van/year; constant charge; predictable; simple
Reducing balance at 30%: Year 1 = £28,000 × 30% = £8,400; Year 2 = £19,600 × 30% = £5,880 — higher early charges
Vans depreciate quickly in early years — reducing balance mirrors this economic reality more accurately
Higher early depreciation reduces reported profit in early years — tax benefits potentially
Straight-line gives more predictable profit figures — easier for financial planning
If Amir wants stable annual charges, straight-line is better; if he wants to match economic reality, reducing balance is better
Conclusion: reducing balance is arguably more appropriate for vehicles that lose value faster in early years; straight-line is simpler and gives stable profit reporting

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one method; minimal analysis.
Calculates charges for both methods; considers advantages of each; partial conclusion.
Well-developed comparison with calculations; considers economic reality, profit impact and simplicity; justified recommendation.

scenario: An investor is considering buying shares in two competing companies: RedCo — GPM 52%, NPM 14%, ROCE 22%, current ratio 1.8:1; BlueCo — GPM 39%, NPM 22%, ROCE 31%, current ratio 0.9:1.
question: Discuss which company the investor should choose. (6)

indicative_content: RedCo: high GPM, positive NPM and ROCE; good liquidity (1.8:1); less efficient at converting gross profit to net profit
BlueCo: lower GPM but higher NPM (22%) — more efficient at controlling expenses; ROCE 31% is significantly better; but current ratio 0.9:1 is below 1 — liquidity risk
From investor perspective: BlueCo generates better returns (ROCE, NPM) but liquidity risk could threaten solvency in short term
RedCo is more liquid and less risky but generates lower returns
Choice depends on investor's risk appetite
Conclusion: BlueCo offers better returns but higher risk; RedCo safer choice for risk-averse investor; risk-seeking investor may prefer BlueCo

level_descriptors.descriptor: States one or two ratios; limited comparison or conclusion.
Compares both companies across multiple ratios; considers return vs risk; partial recommendation.
Thorough comparison; discusses return, liquidity risk and investor perspective; justified recommendation with caveat.

scenario: PolarBrew Ltd brews craft beer. Year 3 income statement: Revenue £900,000; COGS £540,000; Gross profit £360,000; Expenses £270,000; Net profit £90,000. Year 2 NPM was 16%.
question: Discuss the profitability of PolarBrew Ltd and identify two actions management could take to improve performance. (6)

indicative_content: NPM Year 3 = (£90k ÷ £900k) × 100 = 10% — compared to 16% in Year 2; significant decline
Expenses have grown: Year 3 expenses = £270k = 30% of revenue; in Year 2 if NPM was 16% on similar revenue, expenses would have been lower
Possible causes: higher wages, increased overheads, higher rent, depreciation
Actions: 1) Review and reduce overhead costs — negotiate rent or rationalise headcount; 2) Review pricing — can selling price increase to improve GPM?
Revenue growth may be needed — promotional campaigns or new distribution channels
Conclusion: profitability has declined; cost control and/or revenue growth are the priority for management

level_descriptors.descriptor: Calculates one ratio; little analysis of the Year 2 comparison.
Calculates both ratios; compares to Year 2; one developed action.
Full ratio analysis with year-on-year comparison; two well-developed actions; justified conclusion.

topic: F2 SFP / F4 Ratios — working capital
scenario: FastSew Ltd makes bespoke clothing. SFP extract: Inventory £82,000; Receivables £46,000; Cash £12,000; Trade payables £95,000; Tax payable £15,000.
question: Discuss the liquidity position of FastSew Ltd and recommend two actions to improve it. (6)

indicative_content: Current assets = £82k + £46k + £12k = £140,000
Current liabilities = £95k + £15k = £110,000
Current ratio = £140k ÷ £110k = 1.27:1 — above 1 but modest
Acid test = (£140k − £82k) ÷ £110k = £58k ÷ £110k = 0.53:1 — below 1; significant liquidity concern as inventory is large relative to liquid assets
£82k inventory is 59% of current assets — bespoke clothing inventory may be hard to liquidate quickly
Actions: 1) Reduce inventory levels by improving production-to-order efficiency; 2) Chase receivables (£46k outstanding) more aggressively to bring in cash
Conclusion: current ratio is acceptable but acid test reveals underlying concern; reducing inventory and improving debtor collection would significantly improve liquidity

level_descriptors.descriptor: Identifies concern with ratios; minimal analysis.
Calculates current ratio and acid test; identifies inventory issue; one recommendation.
Full liquidity analysis using both ratios; explains inventory concern; two developed recommendations; justified conclusion.

scenario: SunriseFurniture Ltd — Year 3 data: Revenue £1,200,000; COGS £720,000; Gross profit £480,000; Expenses £348,000; Net profit £132,000. SFP: Non-current assets £520,000 (net of depreciation); Inventory £95,000; Receivables £72,000; Cash £18,000; Trade payables £68,000; Bank overdraft £40,000; Long-term loan £200,000; Share capital £200,000; Retained earnings £197,000. Year 2 comparatives: GPM 46%, NPM 14%, ROCE 19%, current ratio 1.9:1.
question: Evaluate the financial performance and position of SunriseFurniture Ltd, comparing Year 3 with Year 2. (12)

indicative_content: GPM Year 3 = (£480k ÷ £1,200k) × 100 = 40% — down from 46%; COGS risen as % of revenue
NPM Year 3 = (£132k ÷ £1,200k) × 100 = 11% — down from 14%; double margin squeeze
Current assets = £95k + £72k + £18k = £185,000; current liabilities = £68k + £40k = £108,000; current ratio = 1.71:1 — down from 1.9:1 but still adequate
Acid test = (£185k − £95k) ÷ £108k = £90k ÷ £108k = 0.83:1 — below 1; some liquidity concern

Capital employed = £520k + £185k − £108k = £597k (or equity + long-term liabilities = £397k + £200k = £597k); ROCE = (£132k ÷ £597k) × 100 = 22.1% — up from 19%; returns per £ of capital have improved despite margin compression
Revenue growth (positive) but both margins declining — cost of sales and/or expenses rising faster
Overdraft is a concern — may indicate cash flow pressure
Receivables at £72k — consider whether debtors are being collected efficiently

Conclusion: revenue and ROCE growth are positives; but margin deterioration and rising overdraft suggest cost pressures and potential working capital strain; management should focus on controlling costs and reducing debtor collection days

level_descriptors.descriptor: Calculates 1-2 ratios; limited year-on-year comparison; isolated observations.
Calculates 3+ ratios; compares to Year 2; addresses both performance and position; partial conclusion.
Balanced evaluation using profit, liquidity and ROCE; compares to Year 2; identifies key strengths and concerns; supported conclusion.

Thorough evaluation of all key ratios with Year 2 comparison; explains underlying causes of changes; addresses profitability, liquidity and capital efficiency; specialist vocabulary throughout; clear, justified conclusion with specific recommendations.

scenario: MediTech Ltd purchased specialist scanning equipment on 1 January Year 1 for £200,000. Estimated useful life: 8 years. Residual value: £8,000. Finance director Priti is choosing between straight-line and reducing balance depreciation at 25% pa. [Year 1 data before depreciation: Revenue £500,000; Gross profit £180,000; Capital employed £600,000. Year 1 comparatives if SL: Depreciation £24,000. If RB: Depreciation £50,000.]
question: Evaluate the impact of each depreciation method on MediTech Ltd's Year 1 financial statements and ratios, and recommend which method to use. (12)

indicative_content: SL: Net profit = £180,000 − £24,000 − other expenses; NPM higher
RB: Net profit = £180,000 − £50,000 − other expenses; NPM lower by £26,000
SL: NBV Year 1 end = £176,000; RB: NBV = £150,000 — lower asset value on SFP under RB
ROCE: SL would show higher net profit therefore higher ROCE; RB lower
Current ratio unaffected (depreciation is non-cash charge)
RB more accurately reflects economic reality for specialist equipment that may depreciate faster
However, SL gives more predictable charges and better reported profitability in early years
If MediTech seeking external finance or investor confidence, SL may present better ratios
Recommendation: SL preferred for simplicity and stable profit reporting unless HMRC tax treatment favours RB; RB better reflects equipment wear pattern

level_descriptors.descriptor: Calculates one depreciation charge; limited comparison of impact.
Calculates both charges; discusses NPM / ROCE impact; partial recommendation.
Quantified evaluation of both methods on NPM, ROCE and SFP; considers investor/lender impact; supported recommendation.

Thorough evaluation with full calculations for both methods; analyses impact on all relevant ratios; considers economic reality vs simplicity, reporting strategy and external stakeholder impact; specialist vocabulary; justified recommendation with acknowledged trade-offs.

topic: F1/F2/F4 Financial statements and ratios — competitor comparison
scenario: Two competing hotel chains — Year 3: [Table: | | SkyLodge PLC | SunStay Ltd | | Revenue | £8.2m | £5.6m | | COGS | £3.3m | £2.0m | | Gross profit | £4.9m | £3.6m | | Expenses | £4.1m | £2.5m | | Net profit | £0.8m | £1.1m | | Current assets | £1.4m | £0.9m | | Inventory | £0.3m | £0.15m | | Current liabilities | £1.1m | £0.45m | | Capital employed | £5.0m | £3.6m |]
question: Evaluate which hotel chain is performing better financially and which you would recommend to a potential investor. (12)

indicative_content: SkyLodge GPM = (£4.9m ÷ £8.2m) × 100 = 59.8%; SunStay GPM = (£3.6m ÷ £5.6m) × 100 = 64.3% — SunStay has better gross margin
SkyLodge NPM = (£0.8m ÷ £8.2m) × 100 = 9.8%; SunStay NPM = (£1.1m ÷ £5.6m) × 100 = 19.6% — SunStay more than doubles SkyLodge on NPM
SkyLodge ROCE = (£0.8m ÷ £5.0m) × 100 = 16%; SunStay ROCE = (£1.1m ÷ £3.6m) × 100 = 30.6% — SunStay significantly better
SkyLodge current ratio = £1.4m ÷ £1.1m = 1.27:1; SunStay = £0.9m ÷ £0.45m = 2.0:1 — SunStay more liquid
SkyLodge acid test = (£1.4m − £0.3m) ÷ £1.1m = 1.0:1; SunStay = (£0.9m − £0.15m) ÷ £0.45m = 1.67:1 — SunStay stronger
SkyLodge: larger revenue but expenses are 50% of revenue (vs SunStay 44.6%) — less efficient cost control
SunStay outperforms on every ratio despite smaller scale
Recommendation: SunStay Ltd is the stronger investment — better profitability, liquidity and capital efficiency; SkyLodge's revenue scale does not translate to superior returns

level_descriptors.descriptor: Calculates 1-2 ratios for one company; limited comparison.
Calculates key ratios for both; identifies SunStay as stronger on some metrics; partial recommendation.
Comparative evaluation using 4+ ratios; analyses profitability and liquidity; supported investor recommendation.

Thorough evaluation of all key ratios for both companies; explains why revenue size is not the key metric; analyses cost efficiency; considers liquidity; specialist vocabulary; clear investor recommendation with acknowledged risks.
